Senses.PreferredTarget: As feelings arise, wisdom is cut off; as thought changes, the underlying nature seems different
AlternateTargets: Feeling blocks wisdom; changing notions make the true basis appear divided
SearchAliases: feeling obscures wisdom thought makes nature seem different
emotion divides wisdom imagination divides nature
Senses.Note: The first clause describes a felt attachment that blocks wisdom. The second says that changing thoughts make the underlying basis appear divided or altered. Masters use the pair to explain why ordinary seeing, hearing, and activity can be missed despite being present. Wanru strikes his staff after it, Hanyu applies it to everyday sense contact, and Shengke warns that even this explanation can become a resting place. The records treat this as a distortion of recognition while the underlying nature remains available.

Senses.Explanation: 情知 means to know full well or to recognize that something is just as expected. In direct exchange it can be “I knew it” or “sure enough”; in commentary it can frame a third person's act or expected reply as predictable, so first person is not built into the expression. In Five Lamps Compendium, Ziman tells a monk, “I knew you were at a loss” (情知汝罔措), while Pingtian Puan tells Linji Yixuan, “I knew you had met an adept” (情知你見作家來). These are different conversations in the same compilation, not two independent source families. Baizhang Le uses the phrase to anticipate a hearer's misconstrual. An unnamed monk in Liangting Jingting's record gives the bare reply 情知, “I knew it,” and Liangting immediately answers him. Shiyu Mingfang says “I knew you would say that” after a monk repeats the criticism he expected, while Baichi Yuan says “I knew you would make that shout” and strikes the monk. Zhongfeng Mingben uses a third-person narrative construction about Bodhidharma before Emperor Wu: he says it was predictable that Bodhidharma would answer “I do not know” (不識) when questioned by the emperor. The common thread is confident recognition; irony, rebuke, and narration are uses of that recognition rather than separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Cognition operating through feeling, sentiment, and recognition: affective or feeling-bound discernment. The term is repeatedly paired with estimating, reckoning, distinguishing, and interpretive understanding. Yuanwu Keqin asks whether a case can be estimated through affective cognition and calls explanations offered in public addresses affective-cognitive reckoning. Xuedou Chongxian says that recognizing the lineage at the words may still remain dim beyond its bounds. Huanglong Fazhong excludes affective-cognitive discrimination from his stated phrase. Liao'an Qingyu contrasts uncontrived writing with people glued to affective cognition and occupied with ornamental composition. Juelang Daosheng criticizes using knowledge and affective cognition to estimate public cases and encounter moves, while Tianru Weize calls what people learn and say dependence on affective cognition and interpretive understanding. The Zen bend is therefore grammatical and public: the records name the cognitive equipment by which students estimate cases and speeches, then explicitly mark that equipment as the obstruction or limit under criticism.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有問：『雲溪病，有不病者麼？』荅他道：『無。』『恁麼則和尚全身病也。』荅他道：『老僧病入膏肓，只覓他起處不得。』一病十五日不起，口巴巴的說甚佛法。古人說渠說我，分明話作兩頭。雲溪老漢零零丁丁，只這個有病的若存若亡，這邊那邊安放不下。何況他不病者，又去好肉穵瘡。他看我卻沒鼻頭，我看他全無眼孔。如今將渠將我打作一塊、束做一團，都送在針鋒眼裏，病與不病且自由他。逢人切忌錯舉。」

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2004.xml). Wansong’s Commentary and Chanting on Tiantong Jue’s Verse-Comments on the Ancients: Record of the Congrong Hermitage. Speaker: Hongzhi Zhengjue. The case's chanted verse as the Hermitage quotes it, writing (捉手) where Hongzhi's own record writes (投手).

Senses.Explanation: (病與不病, sick or not sick) is Daowu's answer to Guishan's visit-the-sick question, born inside Guishan Lingyou's own record: how many are sick? Some sick, some not sick. Is the not-sick one the ascetic Zhi? Sick or not sick, neither concerns him — speak quickly; even saying it has nothing to do with him. Hongzhi Zhengjue raises the exchange and answers it with the wonder-drug verse — the medicine never passed the mouth, the physician cannot lay a hand on it; Wansong Xingxiu gives it a case number in the Congrong Hermitage. Out of the Song formula the Ming and Qing masters grow answers of their own: Weilin Daopei sets one bed, lies sick on it, and lets the empty flowers scatter — sick or not sick, it does not concern him; Hanyue Fazang rises from a whole-body sickness and asks — one body, why two ways?. The root. Guishan asks where Daowu has been — visiting the sick — and how many are sick; some sick, some not. Is the not-sick one the ascetic Zhi? Daowu answers with the formula and Guishan closes: even saying it has nothing to do with him. Wansong's Congrong Hermitage sets the case under the assembly opening on the whole-body sickness Vimalakirti could not cure and the grass Manjusri knows how to use, in a contracted recension whose close drops the graphs (與他). Muchen Daomin, preaching on sickness, quotes the case and widens the formula: if sickness does not concern him, know that birth, old age and death likewise do not — what was it in the old man that so transcended? He strikes the staff, rises, and caps with the couplet on spirit owing nothing to heaven and earth. The commentarial trail. Hongzhi's verse answers the case rather than repeating it: the wonderful medicine never passed the mouth, the divine physician cannot lay a hand on it; if existent it was never absent, if empty never there; unborn yet living, undying yet long-lived. Wuyi Yuanlai names the two elders — Guishan held to benevolence, Daowu to righteousness — and then asks the triple question: who is the sick one, the not-sick one, the unconcerned one? Point him out. The Qing Raising Old Cases anthology carries both nien: Wuyi's triple question again, and Muchen's — a good teacher of fifteen hundred talking like this would get the staff across his spine from me, though that very staff has a falling-short place; check it, worthies. The Qing hall answers. Weilin Daopei, after citing the old saying that sickness is the good medicine of living beings, raises the case and doubles the formula: not only does sickness not concern him, not-sickness also does not concern him; saying it does not, not saying it also does not. Who is he after all? Investigate. Pinjixiang Zhixiang prints the case under Daowu's own section head and follows it with the eulogy on the body too empty for basis or appearance, nowhere to be placed from the first — let the eight winds blow as they will. On their own sickbeds. Weilin's self-mocking poem: the empty chest holds only the four snakes gnawing each other, and the old master of the empty king laughs — sick or not sick, it does not concern him, when did sand ever get into the eye? One bed set, lying sick, letting the riot of empty flowers scatter. Yongjue Yuanxian, tossing in an illness that will not lift, watches how the ten thousand images begin, finds quiet ease, and concludes that sick or not sick, both are utterly groundless. And Weilin's verse for the sick steward Jingbai sets the instruction: the practitioner knows his own sickness, worldly thoughts long forgotten — watch only the not-sick one, sickness returns to the land of nothing-at-all; sick or not sick, both beyond measure. Rising, treating, letting be. Hanyue Fazang, recovered: days ago the whole body was sickness, sickness was sickness and medicine was sickness — who knew there was a not-sick one? Now the fevers have gone somewhere unknown, the three hundred bones and eighty thousand pores shaken clean, no source of sickness to be found. Sick or not sick — what idle talk is this? One body: why two ways?. Zhangxue Tongzui writes for a physician: sitting at the crossroads selling the agada panacea — whoever comes, sick or not sick, pulled up by the root. Liangting Jingting, fifteen days down, is asked whether the sick Yunxi has a not-sick one — none; the sickness has entered the marrow, only its arising-place cannot be found. He bundles self and other into one lump and sends it into the eye of a needle: sick or not sick, he lets it be — when you meet people, above all do not quote this wrongly. The letter. Yunwai Xingze writes to a householder just back from illness: trace sickness to karma and karma to mind; when the mind-source has no arising, what of sickness and karma? The one who receives sickness cannot be found, nor the one that makes it sick — sick or not sick equally unobtainable, knowledge and unknowing likewise forced names. Seen this way the ten directions are gathered entire into this one sickness; hold to that, and it is a single cooling plaster.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase compares an event to sudden thunder that arrives before one can cover one’s ears. Yuanwu Keqin uses it as an appraisal; Wuyong Jingquan places it in a verse about raising a bamboo staff; Wuyi Yuanlai applies it to a sharp question and answer; and Fori Zhicai gives it as an answer. Juelang Daosheng applies the image to an assembly, while an unnamed questioner uses it of Dahui Zonggao’s reply.
